## **TECHNICAL INFORMATION** 

- GlucoPlex contains the herbs Gymnema, Fenugreek and Cinnamon, and nutrients to help support healthy blood sugar. 

- GlucoPlex contains nutrients that assist carbohydrate and sugar metabolism, including alpha Lipoic acid (ALA) and chromium, which are necessary for the cellular uptake of glucose. 

- GlucoPlex contains antioxidant nutrients, ALA, chromium and zinc, that help reduce free radicals formed in the body. Antioxidants help offset the oxidative effects of high sugar. 

- Glucoplex contains nutrients that support insulin production and activity. Insulin is a hormone produced by beta-cells in the pancreas. It is released into the blood stream after a meal, where it transports glucose from the blood stream into the cells for use as energy. 

## Gymnema 

- Gymnema is a herb native to India and Sri Lanka that has a long history of use in Ayurvedic medicine. 

- Gymnema has wide-ranging actions on glucose metabolism. Primarily, it reduces glucose absorption in the blood and stimulates insulin secretion through increased pancreatic beta-cell numbers and improved cell function. In rabbits, Gymnema has also demonstrated improvements in glycogen synthesis, glycolysis, gluconeogenesis and hepatic and muscle glucose uptake[1] . 

- Gymnema contains triterpene saponins, known as Gymnemic acids, and Gymnema saponins, which are believed to be responsible for the herb’s pharmacological activity. GlucoPlex contains Gymnema leaf standardised to contain 25mg of Gymnemic acids. 

- A small study in 10 healthy young adults found that 2g Gymnema three times a day significantly reduced fasting blood sugar levels compared with baseline[2] . 

- Gymnema also has unusual activity where it supresses the perception of the sweet taste on the tongue. Because of this action, it is known as gurmar (sugar destroyer) in Hindi. Gymnemic acids have an atomical arrangement similar in structure to sugar molecules that fill the receptors in the taste buds. Ingestion of Gymnemic acids fills the receptors in the taste buds, preventing their activation by the sugar 

molecule in food. Similarly, in the intestine, Gymnemic acids attach to the receptor present in the intestine, preventing the absorption of sugar molecules into the intestines[3] . 

## Cinnamon 

- Cinnamon increases the uptake of glucose into cells by enhancing insulin receptor phosphorylation and translocation of the glucose transporter GLUT4 to the plasma membrane. It increases the number of GLUT4 receptors and insulin receptors, facilitating glucose entry into cells. 

- In a double-blind study, 79 patients with poor sugar control were randomly assigned to 1g Cinnamon or placebo three times a day for 4 months. Cinnamon significantly reduced plasma glucose by 10.3%[4] . 

- In another study, the addition of 1, 3 or 6g of Cinnamon to the diet significantly decreased serum glucose levels (18-29%) after 40 days. No significant changes were noted in the placebo groups[5] . 

## Fenugreek 

- Fenugreek has been used medicinally for thousands of years in Asia and the Mediterranean. 

- Fenugreek enhances glucose uptake into cells and the utilisation of glucose as energy. It contains 4-hydroxyisoleucine, an amino acid which increases pancreatic insulin secretion and inhibits sucrose α-D-glucosidase and α-amylase[6] . This effect is glucose-dependent and only occurs in the presence of moderate to high glucose concentrations[7] . 

- A 6-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel trial investigated the effect of Fenugreek seed extract on eating behaviours in 39 healthy overweight males. Fenugreek consumption significantly decreased insulin/glucose ratio relative to placebo (p=0.044)[8] . 

- Another double-blind, placebo-controlled study found that 1g/day of Fenugreek seed significantly decreased area under curve (AUC) of blood glucose and insulin (p<0.001)[9] . Fenugreek increased insulin sensitivity and improved glycaemic control.

## Chromium 

- Chromium facilitates the entry of glucose into cells by stimulating insulin uptake and enhancing its activity[10] . 

- Evidence shows that insulin is more effective in the presence of chromium. Inside the cell, four chromium ions bind with the molecule apochromodulin, forming chromodulin, which binds to the insulin receptor, increasing receptor activity.

- Chromium is a constituent of the ‘Glucose Tolerance Factor’, the biologically active form of chromium that is involved in glucose metabolism. 

- Chromium requirements are increased when consuming a diet high in sugar. 

## Nutrients 

- ALA is a unique, fat and water-soluble antioxidant that enhances cellular glucose uptake and utilisation. In conjunction with exercise, ALA can enhance glucose transport and insulin signalling in skeletal muscle cells. 

- Vitamin D is essential for normal insulin secretion in humans. Vitamin D receptors are found in pancreatic beta-cells. 

- Zinc has antioxidant activity and is found in high concentrations in the pancreas where it has both endocrine and exocrine functions. It is required for the normal synthesis, storage and secretion of insulin in pancreatic beta-cells. Zinc also stimulates glycolysis, inhibits gluconeogenesis and plays a role in glucose transport in adipocytes[11] . 

## **DRUG INTERACTIONS** 

- Caution with hypoglycaemic medications and insulin – GlucoPlex may have additive effects. Monitor. 

- Caution with warfarin – ALA has reduced platelet reactivity in vitro, uncertain whether the effect is clinically significant. 

- Caution with anticoagulant/antiplatelet drugs – Fenugreek may have additive effects, increasing the risk of bruising and bleeding. 

- Caution with thyroxine – ALA may suppress the conversion of thyroxine to active T3 form and chromium can reduce thyroxine absorption. Separate dose by 3 hours. 

- Caution with calcium channel blockers – vitamin D may reduce the effectiveness of these drugs. 

- Caution with digoxin – vitamin D can elevate serum calcium levels, which increases the risk of cardiac arrhythmias with digoxin. Monitor calcium levels. 

- Caution with thiazide diuretics – when taken in conjunction with vitamin D, can increase the risk of hypercalcaemia. Monitor serum calcium levels during concurrent use. 

- Caution with cholestyramine or colestipol (lipid-lowering medication) and orlistat – these drugs may reduce the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, including vitamin D. Take one hour before, or 4-6 hours after drug. 

- Caution with NSAIDs, cefalexin, penicillamine and tetracycline and quinolone antibiotics - zinc forms complexes with these drugs, interfering with absorption. Separate dose by 3 hours. 

- Caution with iron supplements – Fenugreek and zinc can interfere with iron absorption. Separate dose by 2 hours. 

- Caution with copper and manganese supplementation – ALA can bind to minerals. Separate dose by 3 hours. 

## **CAUTIONS** 

- Contraindicated during pregnancy and lactation. 

- Contraindicated in sarcoidosis or hyperparathyroidism without medical supervision. 

## **SIDE EFFECTS** 

- Fenugreek may cause mild gastrointestinal symptoms, such as diarrhoea, bloating and flatulence. 

- Gymnema and Fenugreek are rich in saponins, which may cause irritation of the gastric mucous membranes and reflux.

Figure 1: Knee joint 

- Glucosamine is a component of glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans of the cartilage matrix and is required for the production of proteoglycans, mucopolysaccharides and hyaluronic acid. These substances form joint tissue, such as articular cartilage, tendons and synovial fluid. 

- Exogenous glucosamine exists in two forms - glucosamine hydrochloride (HCl) and glucosamine sulfate. Glucosamine sulfate requires compound stabilisers in the form of salts and has 74% purity. Glucosamine HCl lacks the sulfate group and has 99% purity, providing a higher percentage of glucosamine compared to sulfate forms[1] . 

- Chondroitin belongs to a class of polymers known as glucosaminoglycans and act as the flexible connecting matrix between cartilage and connective tissue. 

- Methylsulfonylmethane (MSM) is a naturally occurring source of sulfur. Sulfur is a component of many tissues in the body and plays a role in the development and maintenance of connective tissue. 

## Joints 

- A joint is an articulation where two bones meet that allows for mobility. Joints are complex structures comprised of bone, muscles, synovium, cartilage and ligaments designed to bear weight and facilitate movement. 

- Joints are cushioned by cartilage and lubricated with synovial fluid to allow movement and twisting freely without pain. The principal lubricating substances in cartilage, tendons, ligaments, synovial fluid and mucous membranes are proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans (GAGs). 

- Cartilage is a type of tissue that covers the surface of a bone at a joint and helps reduce friction of movement within a joint. The synovial membrane lines the joint and seals the joint capsule by secreting synovial fluid, a clear, sticky substance that lubricates the joint. 

- Ligaments connect bones together and are composed of tough connective tissue surrounding the joint to provide support and limit the joint’s movement. Tendons are another type of connective tissue and connect muscle to bones. 

## Joint health 

- Glucosamine MAX helps support joint cartilage health and maintains joint health. 

- Glucosamine is required for the synthesis of glycoproteins, glycolipids and GAGs and stimulates metabolism of chondrocytes in the articular cartilage and synovial cells in the synovial tissues. 

- Chondroitin is endogenously found in cartilaginous tissues and serves as a substrate for the formation of the joint matrix structure. It can protect cartilage by inhibiting elastase and hyaluronidase enzymes that damage joint cartilage. 

- MSM is an organic form of sulfur that, together with glucosamine, is required for the production of important structural components of joint cartilage by cross-linkages through disulphide bonds. GAGs, the fundamental building blocks of joint cartilage, are linked together by disulfide bonds, making cartilage firm and resilient. 

- Glycine and proline are amino acids required for the biosynthesis of collagen and elastin, important for healthy cartilage production and joint health. Proline is a major amino acid found in cartilage. 

- Silica is necessary for the normal growth and development of connective tissue and is abundant in bones, hair, skin and nails. Silica is required for the cross-linking of collagen strands, important for the strength and integrity of the connective tissue matrix. Collagen is the most abundant protein found in the body and is responsible for maintaining the integrity of tendons, ligaments and cartilage.

## Mild osteoarthritis 

- Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common type of arthritis and is characterised by the degeneration of the joint cartilage that is responsible for the protection of the bone ends and joint. The deterioration of cartilage causes the surfaces of bones to become pitted and irregular, causing friction. 

- OA predominantly affects the weight-bearing joints such as the knees, hips and back, but can also affect the hands and knuckles. Tendons, ligaments and muscles surrounding the joint weaken and the joint becomes distorted, inflamed, painful and stiff. 

- Glucosamine MAX relieves symptoms of mild osteoarthritis including 

- mild joint pain, stiffness and inflammation. 

- Glucosamine may affect the cytokine-mediated pathways that regulate inflammation, cartilage degradation and immune responses. It can reduce or regulate interleukin-1 (IL-1) levels in synovial fluid and inhibits the actions of catabolic enzymes in the joint. This reduces inflammation and cartilage degradation, potentially altering the progression of OA[2] . 

- The forms of glucosamine and chondroitin found in Glucosamine MAX match those used in GAIT (Glucosamine/chondroitin Arthritis Intervention Trial), the first large-scale clinical trial to determine the effects of the dietary supplements glucosamine hydrochloride (glucosamine) and sodium chondroitin sulfate (chondroitin sulfate) for knee OA. The multicentre double-blind, placebo and celecoxib-controlled GAIT trial randomly assigned 1583 patients with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis to receive either glucosamine hydrochloride, chondroitin sulfate, a combination of glucosamine hydrochloride and chondroitin sulfate, celecoxib (Celebrex) or placebo for 24 weeks. For patients with moderate-to-severe pain at baseline, the rate of response was significantly higher with the combined therapy of glucosamine hydrochloride and chondroitin sulfate daily than with placebo[3] . 

- A 2018 meta-analysis systematically reviewed 19 randomised control trials (RCTs) to evaluate the efficacy of glucosamine supplementation in individuals with knee OA. Overall, 12 studies (67%) concluded glucosamine had a significant effect on the symptoms of OA. Positive outcomes on quality of life (including pain alleviation and improved joint mobility and stiffness) were measured using JKOM and WOMAC scores (osteoarthritis symptom and pain scales). The duration of studies varied from 6 weeks to 2 years, with a dose 1500mg/day most commonly used[4] . 

The authors concluded that glucosamine hydrochloride can resolve knee degenerative OA and has symptom-relieving and joint functionimproving action[6] . 

- Glucosamine supplementation (1500mg/day) has been found to be 

- as effective as ibuprofen in the symptomatic relief of OA[7] . 

- Glucosamine MAX also contains 1g Ginger per tablet. Ginger has demonstrated anti-inflammatory activity and helps relieve inflammation. Zingibain, a proteolytic enzyme present in Ginger, is one of the constituents responsible for its anti-inflammatory action. Mechanistic studies have shown that Ginger suppresses prostaglandin synthesis by inhibiting cyclooxygenase-1 and cyclooxygenase-2 and leukotrienes by inhibiting 5-lipoxygenase[8] . 

- The effect of 1g/day of Ginger supplementation on proinflammatory cytokines was investigated in a RCT in 120 individuals with OA. Daily administration for 3 months decreased serum tumour necrosis factor-α and interleukin-1β compared to baseline and relative to placebo[9] . 

- A meta-analysis conducted in 2015 systematically reviewed five RCTs involving 593 subjects to assess the clinical efficacy of oral Ginger for the symptomatic relief of OA. Ginger resulted in a statistically significant reduction in pain and disability compared to placebo. Dosages ranged from 500-1000mg/day of Ginger extract[10] .

## Gout 

- Gout is a type of arthritis caused by too much uric acid in the blood stream. Uric acid is a normal waste product in the body formed when the body breaks down purines from foods. Normally, uric acid dissolves in the blood and is eliminated via the kidneys in urine. However, in individuals with gout, uric acid is not eliminated efficiently and can build up in the bloodstream (hyperuricaemia), forming urate crystals, which lodge in a joint. 

- Gout most often affects the big toe, but can occur in the feet, ankles, 

- knees, wrists and fingers. 

- Symptoms of gout include intense joint pain, swelling and red and shiny skin over the joint. 

- While other types of arthritis develop slowly, an attack of gout happens suddenly, often overnight. 

- Gout affects far more men than women and may have a genetic component. 

- Dietary modification is important for people who suffer from gout as several foods can trigger an attack. Foods high in purines, such as red meats, yeast, poultry, organ meats, fish and shellfish and alcohol should be avoided. Spinach, asparagus, beans, lentils and mushrooms also contain moderate amounts of purines. A wellbalanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, wholegrains, low-fat dairy and adequate water intake is beneficial. 

## Ayuric[®] 

- Ayuric[®] is proprietary ingredient derived from the edible fruits of Terminalia bellirica, an ancient Ayurvedic plant. 

- Ayuric[®] is both antioxidant and anti-inflammatory, while also having been clinically studied to lower uric acid levels in individuals with hyperuricemia. Ayuric[®] is postulated to work by inhibiting xanthine oxidase (XO), the enzyme responsible for synthesising uric acid in the body. 

- In a study, 110 eligible subjects with hyperuricemia were randomised to receive either 250mg or 500mg of Ayuric[®] twice daily for a duration of 24 weeks. Serum uric acid levels were measured at baseline and at the end of 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 and 24 weeks. Both active treatment groups showed a reduction in serum uric acid levels compared to baseline[1] . 

- In a further study, 59 subjects were randomised to receive either 500mg or 1000mg of Ayuric[®] twice-daily. Biomarkers of oxidativestress, endothelial function, systemic inflammation, and plateletaggregation were evaluated at baseline, 4, 8, 12 and 24 weeks. Significant improvements in oxidative stress biomarkers and systemic inflammation biomarkers were observed in both groups. The study also demonstrated both doses significantly decreased serum uric acid levels and creatinine levels, while improving glomerular filtration rate over a 24-week period[2] . 

## Celery & Alfalfa 

- Celery is traditionally used in WHM to relieve the symptoms of gout and help reduce the occurrence of gout attacks. 

- Celery is also used in traditional WHM as a diuretic to enhance urine output, and can therefore assist in the clearance of uric acid from the body. 

- Celery contains phthalide derivatives, tannins and phenolic compounds that contribute to its uricosuric action (increased excretion of uric acid in the urine). 

- Apigenin, a flavonoid found in celery, has hyperuricemic and XO inhibitory activity with reports it can interact with the XO active site and is comparable to allopurinol in vitro[3] . 

- Alfalfa is traditionally used in WHM as an anti-arthritic and diuretic to relieve fluid retention. It increases urine production, provides nutritional support and has a general tonic effect.

## **TECHNICAL INFORMATION** 

- Grape Seed Gold is a high potency antioxidant complex containing a unique blend of herbal and nutritional antioxidants to reduce free radical production in the body and support general health and wellbeing. 

- Oxidation is a chemical reaction that can produce free radicals in the body. These free radicals can start a chain reaction that potentially leads to damage within DNA, proteins and lipids in cell membranes. 

- Free radicals are unstable, electrically charged molecules that gain stability by stealing electrons from other molecules, such as proteins, DNA and cell membranes through the oxidation process. When oxidation occurs, important components of cells become damaged and lose their ability to function normally. Oxidative damage can eventually lead to cell death and is considered to play a role in many health conditions and the acceleration of the ageing process. 

- Oxidation is a natural reaction within the body, but increased oxidation can be caused by several internal or external factors, including stress, environmental chemicals, cigarette smoking, alcohol, poor diet, sunlight, pollution and excessive exercise. 

- Antioxidants can be found in the form of nutrients from fruits and vegetables, as well as phytochemicals found in plants, particularly seeds and bark, where they help to combat free radical damage by donating one of their electrons to a free radical molecule to inhibit the oxidation process and prevent cell damage. 

- Grape Seed Gold supports healthy eyesight and vision and helps maintain healthy immune system function. 

## Grape seed quality 

- Grape Seed Gold contains a non-GMO Grape seed extract sourced exclusively from the Champagne region of France, well-known for its premium quality wine. Due to the high prevalence of adulterated Grape seed extracts, this extract has been validated and verified for its identity, authenticity and quality. 

- The Champagne grapes are cultivated and seasonally harvested in the summer and autumn months, and then either sun or air dried after harvesting. The seeds then undergo extraction, using only water and alcohol without using any harsh solvents or excipients. Quality control process involve microbial testing and testing for environmental contaminants including pesticides and heavy metals. 

- Grape seed is a rich source of proanthocyanidins (PACs) also referred to as procyanidins. Proanthocyanidins are mixtures of oligomeric (2-8 molecules) or polymeric (>9 molecules) flavonoids. Oligomeric procyanidins (OPCs) are made up of dimers and trimers of (+)-catechin or (-)- epicatechin. 

- Specific testing methods have been developed to determine the levels of oligomeric proanthocyanidins (OPCs). Herbs of Gold utilises HPLC analytical to test for total monomers, dimers, trimers, oligomers, oligomeric procyanidins and proanthocyanidins. 

- Grape Seed Gold contains high-strength Grape seed and is standardised to contain 237.5mg of procyanidins per tablet.

- Grape Seed Gold is an antioxidant that helps reduce free radicals formed in the body.

## **TECHNICAL INFORMATION** 

- Gut Care helps maintain a healthy digestive system. It contains anti-inflammatory and demulcent herbs that relieve irritation and inflammation and promote healing in the gastrointestinal tract. 

## Intestinal barrier integrity 

- The intestinal mucosal barrier is a single layer of cells lining the gut that mainly consists of the enterocyte membranes and tight junctions between the enterocytes. The intestinal epithelium acts as a selective barrier, allowing essential dietary nutrients, electrolytes and water from the intestinal lumen into circulation while preventing the passage of unwanted substances, such as food antigens, endotoxins and harmful microorganisms. 

- Loss of intestinal barrier integrity is associated with food allergies, inflammation of the bowel and irritable bowel syndrome. Stress, pathogenic organisms and infections can all weaken intestinal integrity. 

- Healthy intestinal barrier integrity is essential for both digestive health and immune health. 

## L-Glutamine 

- L-Glutamine is the naturally occurring form of the amino acid glutamine. Glutamine is a conditionally essential amino acid. Usually, human cells can readily synthesise the amino acid, however, under certain physiological conditions, the body’s tissues need more glutamine than can be supplied by the diet and biosynthesis and supplementation becomes necessary. Catabolic stress can deplete cellular glutamine by more than 50 percent. 

- L-Glutamine supports digestive health and immune health. It is an important fuel source for the rapidly dividing cells of the gastrointestinal system and the immune system, particularly lymphocytes and monocytes. The gastrointestinal tract is the greatest user of glutamine in the body as glutamine is the principle metabolic fuel of enterocytes. 

- Glutamine is essential for maintaining intestinal barrier function and immune responses. In vitro and in vivo research shows that glutamine aids in the proliferation and repair of intestinal cells and is, therefore, essential for maintaining the integrity of the intestinal lining and preventing the translocation of microbes and endotoxins into 

the body[1] . Animal studies have shown that glutamine can decrease intestinal permeability and help heal damage to the gut wall[2] . Glutamine supports intestinal barrier function by regulating tight junction protein expression and intestinal immunity. 

- Glutamine is also involved in the synthesis of glutathione, an important antioxidant and hepatic detoxifier. 

## DGL Licorice 

- Licorice has a long history, over 3000 years, of medicinal use. In Roman times, Marcellus Empiricus (5[th] century AD) suggested the use of Licorice to treat many disturbances or pathologies of the stomach and intestine and indigestion[3] . Licorice is a demulcent to soothe gastrointestinal tract mucous membranes. 

- Licorice also has anti-inflammatory and mucoprotective activity. It helps protect the gastrointestinal tract by stimulating the secretion of mucin, the protective substance that lines the stomach and intestines. 

- Gut Care contains deglycyrrhizinated Licorice (DGL), which contains less than 3.5% glycyrrhizin. Glycyrrhizin is the active constituent that is responsible for the majority of the side effects associated with Licorice root. DGL can be consumed long-term without the side-effects associated with glycyrrhizin. 

## Aloe vera, Calendula & Slippery elm 

- Aloe vera and Slippery elm are demulcent herbs that soothe irritation and inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract. Gut Care contains Aloe vera leaf inner juice which is the clear gel or mucilage produced by the inner parenchymal cells in the central part of the Aloe vera leaf. It does not contain any latex, which contains anthraquinones and has stimulant laxative activity. 

- Slippery elm bark contains mucilage, which coats the surface of mucous membranes and forms a protective gel-like layer that soothes irritated and inflamed tissues. It is traditionally used to relieve gastrointestinal tract inflammation and irritation. 

- Calendula is traditionally used as an anti-inflammatory to help 

- relieve inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract. 

- Aloe vera and Calendula are traditionally used as vulnerary herbs to help heal the upper gastrointestinal tract.

- Gut Care helps maintain healthy immune system function and healthy gastrointestinal immunity. ## **DRUG INTERACTIONS** 

- Theoretically, Slippery elm may slow the absorption and reduce serum levels of orally administered drugs due to its mucilage content. Clinical significance is unclear. Caution is warranted with drugs with a narrow therapeutic range (e.g. barbiturates, digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, warfarin). Separate dose by 2 hours.

- Caution with glucose lowering medications (including metformin) – Aloe vera given in conjunction with glucose-lowering medication may have additive effects. Potentially beneficial interaction.

## Cardiovascular system 

- The cardiovascular system comprises three essential components: the heart, the blood and blood vessels consisting of veins, arteries and capillaries. It functions to transport nutrients, oxygen and hormones to cells throughout the body and remove metabolic waste. 

## Cardiovascular health

## Hayfever & sinusitis 

- Hayfever is a commonly used term for allergic rhinitis, which is simply an allergy that affects the eyes and nose. Sinusitis occurs because of inflammation or swelling of the passages within the nose, that can also frequently be caused by allergies. 

- According to Allergy & Anaphylaxis Australian, 20% of Australian adults suffer from hayfever[1] . Hayfever occurs when the body’s natural immune defence mechanism overreacts to normal everyday substances such as pollens, grasses, dust mites, animal dander, foods or mold, identifying them as allergens. As a result of this exposure, the immune system becomes hypersensitive, triggering IgE (immunoglobulins) antibodies that secrete excessive amounts of white blood cells (basophils and mast cells), which enter the blood stream as a form of defence. 

- IgE antibodies bind to the mast cells which contain histamine, and as the mast cells are stimulated by the allergen, large amounts of histamine and other inflammatory mediators are released into the blood stream producing an allergic reaction cascade with symptoms such as itching, swelling, inflammation and excessive mucus production[2] . Dampening the effects of histamine during an allergic reaction helps to relieve these symptoms. 

- Hayfever, or allergic rhinitis, is a common condition with symptoms similar to the common cold, such as sneezing, congestion, runny nose, itchy throat as well as a dry or wet, irritating cough. 

- Allergies are chronic in nature and may be seasonal or perennial. Seasonal allergies peak during spring and summer when pollen levels are high, whereas perennial allergies occur all year long and 

may be attributed to animal dander, mold, dust mites and other allergens. Respiratory allergies tend to manifest as hayfever (allergic rhinitis) and sinusitis with nasal congestion, itchy, watery eyes and sneezing. ## Oestrogen 

- Oestrogen is a sex hormone with many roles in the body. It is important for cardiovascular and bone health and for the maintenance of healthy skin and blood vessels. In women, oestrogen is responsible for the development of secondary sex characteristics, the female pattern of body fat around the abdomen, hips and breast and the appearance of axillary and pubic hair. In men, oestrogen is essential for the regulation of testosterone and reproductive function, including sperm health. Having too much or too little oestrogen can cause a range of health problems in both males and females. 

- Oestrogen is an umbrella-term for three endogenous oestrogens: oestradiol (E2), oestrone (E1) and oestriol (E3). Oestradiol (secreted from the ovaries/testes) is the most biologically potent oestrogen. In contrast, oestrone (synthesised by the ovaries and peripheral tissue) and oestriol (produced by the metabolism of oestradiol and oestrone in extra-ovarian tissue) are only weakly oestrogenic. 

- Oestrogen levels are controlled by tightly coordinated feedback loops. In women, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) stimulates the follicle to produce oestrogen; a rise in oestrogen shuts off the production of FSH and a fall turns it back on again. Androgens, hormones produced by the testes, ovaries and adrenal cortex, can be converted to oestrogens via the activity of aromatase enzymes. 

- Oestrogen acts on tissues by binding to oestrogen receptors, found particularly in the brain, heart, breast, bone and genital tract. One of the main functions of oestrogen is to stimulate cellular proliferation in cells with oestrogen receptors. Additionally, the presence of oestrogen increases the number of oestrogen receptors on each cell. Therefore, in an oestrogen-rich environment, there are many more cells produced and they also contain more oestrogen receptors, which leads to an escalating ability for oestrogen to stimulate cell growth. Oestrogens circulate in the body bound to sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG), however, only unbound oestrogens can bind to oestrogen receptors and exert a biological effect. 

## Xeno-oestrogens 

- In addition to endogenous oestrogens (produced in the body), humans are also exposed to exogenous oestrogens in the form of phyto-oestrogens and environmental xeno-oestrogens. Phyto-oestrogens are derived from plants and weakly mimic the activity of oestrogen in the body, with potential health benefits. Xeno-oestrogens, on the other hand, strongly mimic the activity of oestrogen in the body and are detrimental to health. Xenooestrogens are often referred to as ‘endocrine disrupters’ and are stored in fat cells. Exposure to environmental oestrogens begins in utero and they persist in the body for decades, with their levels continuing to accumulate over time. 

- Sources of exogenous oestrogens include oral contraceptives and hormone replacement therapy and environmental toxins found in pesticides, herbicides, refrigerants, industrial solvents and plastics that are structurally similar to oestrogen. One of the main sources of exogenous oestrogen is from bisphenol A (BPA), which is a chemical used in the lining of some food and beverage packaging. Small amounts of BPA can migrate from containers into food and drink. Exogenous oestrogens also include hormones used to fatten livestock and promote milk production that enter the body via the food chain. 

## Liver detoxification 

- The main route of oestrogen metabolism and elimination is via the liver, so healthy liver function is essential for the detoxification and clearance of oestrogen from the body. Liver herbs, such as St Mary’s thistle and Rosemary, may help the breakdown of excess oestrogen. 

- Phase I detoxification utilises cytochrome P450 enzymes and involves oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis, hydration or dehalogenation reactions. Toxins are either neutralised and excreted or transformed into intermediary metabolites that enter phase II. Phase II detoxification involves conjugation reactions (including glutathione conjugation, glycine conjugation, methylation, sulphation, glucuronidation and acetylation) to make toxic compounds watersoluble and ready for excretion in the urine or bile. 

- Antioxidants are an essential part of detoxification as they support phase II detoxification and reduce exposure to reactive intermediates produced during phase I. 

- Poor liver function and inadequate oestrogen excretion may result in excess circulating oestrogens.

## **Hormone Metabolism** 

## Oestrogen metabolism 

- Oestrogen is metabolised primarily in the liver though phase I (hydroxylation) and phase II (methylation, glucuronidation and sulfation) liver detoxification and is excreted in the urine and faeces. 

- Phase I (hydroxylation) utilises cytochrome P450 enzymes to produce three intermediary oestrogen metabolites: 2-hydroxyoestrone (2OH), 16α-hydroxyoestrone (16α-OH) or 4-hydroxyoestrone (4-OH). The 2-OH metabolites confer a very weak oestrogenic activity and have a protective role (“good oestrogen”) while the 16α-OH and 4-OH metabolites show persistent oestrogenic activity and promote cellular proliferation and DNA damage (“bad oestrogen”). Women who metabolise more oestrogen via the 16α-OH pathway have an elevated risk of oestrogen-related problems. Therapeutically, the goal is to shift the oestrogen balance towards a less oestrogenic state via the promotion of the 2-OH pathway. The ideal ratio between 2-OH and 16-OH is 2.0. A low ratio (reduced 2-OH) indicates a state of oestrogen excess. 

- During phase II liver detoxification, oestrogens are conjugated via methylation, sulphation and glucuronidation to render the oestrogen more soluble, and therefore more readily excreted in the urine and bile. Conjugated oestrogens cannot bind to oestrogen receptors and do not have any oestrogen activity. 

- Broccoli sprouts, St Mary’s thistle, Rosemary and flavonoids (quercetin) can induce phase II liver detoxification and help support healthy pathways of oestrogen metabolism.

- Oestrogen dominance is implicated in premenstrual syndrome, endometriosis, fibroids, polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), fibrocystic breasts, premature bone loss, hormonal cellular proliferation and immune dysfunction. 

## Broccoli sprout 

- Broccoli is a cruciferous vegetable (part of the brassicacaea family) that supports liver detoxification and healthy metabolism of oestrogen. Cruciferous vegetables include brussel sprouts, broccoli, cabbage, kale, turnips, collards and cauliflower and contain different constituents, including indole-3-carbinol (I3C) and diinolylmethane (DIM), which activate enzymes that increase the rate at which the liver detoxifies and clears oestrogen and promotes the conversion of oestrogen into the less active forms (2-OH). Indole-3-carbinol can also competitively inhibit oestrogen[2] . 

- Studies have found that adding 500g/day Broccoli to the diet can shift oestrogen metabolism and increase the 2-OH:16α-OH ratio. In a study of 34 postmenopausal women, brassica vegetable consumption was associated with a statistically significant increase in 2-OH:16α-OH values, such that for each 10g/day increase in Brassica consumption, there was an increase in the 2-OH:16α-OH ratio of 0.08[3] . 

- Broccoli sprouts are a rich source of glucoraphanin, which is hydrolyzed by myrosinase in the gut to the biologically active sulforaphane. Sulforaphane induces phase II detoxification and antioxidant enzymes by increasing cellular glutathione levels. 

- Interestingly, research has found that 3-day old sprouts of cultivars of certain crucifers, including Broccoli, contain 10–100 times higher levels of glucoraphanin than the corresponding mature plants[4] . 

- A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial investigated the effect of 5g or 10g of Broccoli sprout powder (equivalent to 2 or 4 capsules of Hormone Metabolism) on oxidative stress. At the higher dose, Broccoli sprout powder significantly decreased malondialdehyde (8.9%; p=0.001), oxidised LDL cholesterol (4.9%; p=0.03) and oxidative stress index (13.7%; p=0.001) and significantly increased total antioxidant capacity (15.9%; p=0.001)[5] .

## Oestrogen dominance 

- Oestrogen dominance can occur when too much oestrogen is manufactured, or excess oestrogen is not cleared efficiently from the body. This can cause cell proliferation in oestrogen-dependent tissues, affecting cellular differentiation and altering gene expression. 16α-OH and 4-OH have been associated with genotoxic effects, while 2-OH may induce apoptosis and inhibit cell proliferation[1] . Oestrogen dominance can also cause imbalance in the ratio of oestrogen:progesterone or oestrogen:testosterone. Elevated oestradiol can decrease the production of testosterone via negativefeedback mechanisms. In men, testosterone levels decline with age, however, oestrogen levels remain stable, which results in a change in the testosterone/oestrogen ratio. 

- Body builders who use testosterone-like supplements (including anabolic steroids) to increase their testosterone levels will have increased oestrogen levels. Exogenous testosterone supplementation in men can lead to reduced endogenous production and hormonal imbalance.

Silybin is considered to be the main active component responsible for the herb’s liver-protective effects. Silybin has strong antioxidant activity and helps prevent toxins from crossing the cell membrane, preventing damage to liver cells. Traditionally, St Mary’s thistle is used in Western herbal medicine as a liver tonic and hepatoprotectant.

## **TECHNICAL INFORMATION** 

- Iodine is an essential trace element that is required for healthy thyroid function and for normal growth and development. It also has antioxidant effects, with the ability to donate an electron to decrease damage due to oxygen free radicals. 

- The major food sources of iodine are of marine origin, including kelp and seafood, and fortified salt. Dietary and supplemental iodine is well absorbed, with about 90% of ingested iodine absorbed. Iodine can also be absorbed through the skin. Deficiency occurs when not enough iodine is consumed in the diet. 

- In Australia, many people do not consume adequate iodine. The iodine content of most foods is low, and can be affected by soil levels, irrigation and fertilisers. 

- Two public health measures were introduced in Australia between 2009 and 2010 to reduce iodine deficiency. Food Standards Australia and New Zealand (FSANZ) introduced mandatory fortification of iodised salt used in breadmaking and the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) released a public statement in 2010 recommending that all women who are pregnant, breastfeeding or considering pregnancy, supplement with 150 micrograms iodine daily[1] . 

## Thyroid health 

- Iodine supports thyroid gland health and assists thyroid hormone production. It is essential for the production of the thyroid hormones thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), which influence growth, tissue metabolism and thermogenesis. The thyroid gland stores 80% of the body’s iodine pool and iodine comprises 65% of T4 and 59% of T3. Thyroid hormones are involved in carbohydrate and fat metabolism, in protein synthesis and regulating basal metabolic rate. 

- Thyroid function is regulated by thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), secreted by the pituitary gland. TSH secretion increases uptake of iodine in the thyroid and stimulates the synthesis and release of T3 and T4. Where there is insufficient iodine, TSH levels remain elevated, which can eventually lead to enlargement of the thyroid gland, known as a goitre, and symptoms of hypothyroidism. 

- Symptoms of hypothyroidism include: 

- Weakness, tiredness and sleepiness 

- Dry skin 

- Cold intolerance 

- Hair loss 

- Poor memory and concentration 

- Constipation 

- Reduced appetite and weight gain 

- Due to its role in thyroid hormone production, iodine supports nervous system health and is essential for the proper functioning of the brain and the entire nervous system. 

## Goitrogens 

- Goitrogens are substances that interfere with iodine utilisation, uptake into the thyroid or thyroid hormone production. 

- Goitrogens are present in raw cruciferous vegetables including cabbage, kale, cauliflower, broccoli, turnips and Brussels sprouts, and in linseed, cassava, millet and soy. Cooking these foods deactivates the goitrogens. Certain chemicals from industry or cosmetics can also be classed as goitrogens. 

- Iodine supplementation should be separated from goitrogens in order to maximise absorption. Soy, in particular, can inhibit iodine absorption and high levels of soy isoflavones, genistein and daidzein, can inhibit T3 and T4 production. 

## Pregnancy 

- Iodine is an essential nutrient during pregnancy. Adequate maternal iodine is essential for the development of the foetal brain and nervous system, as it is necessary for the growth of nerve cells, formation of synapses and myelination. 

- During early pregnancy, the foetal thyroid gland development is incomplete, so the foetus is entirely dependent on maternal T4, and therefore on maternal iodine intake. Thyroid hormone production increases by 50% during early pregnancy and renal excretion of iodine increases by 30-50%. In later pregnancy, iodine passes the placenta for foetal thyroid hormone production. The foetal thyroid gland develops by 10-12 weeks of gestation and is capable of thyroid hormone production by approximately 16-20 weeks[2] . 

- Dietary iodine requirements increase by approximately 50% during pregnancy, driven by increased thyroid synthetic demand, increased renal iodine clearance and transfer of iodine to the foetus. National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) guidelines recommend that the daily intake of iodine increase from 150 micrograms/day to 220 micrograms/day during pregnancy[3] . 

- In Australia, it is recommended that pregnant women take an iodine supplement of 150 micrograms/day to reduce risks to the foetus associated with iodine deficiency[4] . In individuals with low iodine status, periconceptional supplementation of 150-290 micrograms/ day is recommended[5] . 

- After birth, babies who are breast-fed will exclusively get their iodine from mother’s milk. Thus, it is essential that breastfeeding women maintain adequate iodine levels to support their health and that of their baby’s. Higher iodine levels are required during lactation, with recommendations between 250 and 290 micrograms/day[6] . 

- It is recommended iodine supplementation start before conception and to continue throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding in order to maintain adequate iodine levels.

## **TECHNICAL INFORMATION** 

- Liver Care contains four liver herbs plus nutrients to support healthy liver function and assist the breakdown of dietary fats. 

- Liver Care contains St Mary’s thistle and Curcumin, potent antioxidants to reduce free radical damage in the body. 

## Liver & gallbladder 

- The liver is the largest internal organ of the human body, weighing 1.5Kg in the average adult. Situated on the upper right side of the abdomen just below the diaphragm, it is protected by the rib cage. It has two sections, the right and the left lobe, separated by the falciform ligament. 

- The liver has several important functions in the body. It has a key role in detoxification, breaking down chemicals, metabolising drugs and removing toxins from the body. It also filters the blood from the digestive system, processes nutrients from the diet and helps regulate body metabolism. It converts carbohydrates into glucose for use as an energy source, and converts glucose into glycogen, to store energy. The liver produces bile, which is stored in the gall bladder, to break down dietary fats and assist in the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, including vitamins A, D, E and K. 

- The gallbladder is a small sac that sits under the liver and stores the bile produced by the liver. It extracts water from its store of bile, concentrating the liquid. The presence of fatty foods triggers the gallbladder to release bile into the intestine to help digest the fat. 

- Poor diet, especially a high fat diet, and excess alcohol or medication use can affect the biliary system. Some common symptoms of poor liver function include nausea, especially after a high fat meal, fatigue, pale stools, itchy skin and jaundice. 

## Liver function 

- Liver Care contains four herbs plus nutrients to support healthy liver function and maintain liver health. 

- St Mary’s thistle is traditionally used in Western herbal medicine (WHM) to support healthy liver function and to protect the liver. Eclectic physicians in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries used St Mary’s thistle for “congestion of the liver, spleen and kidneys”[1] . 

- It is believed that St Mary’s thistle’s hepatoprotective effect is achieved, at least in part, via its antioxidant mechanisms. Silymarin, the herbs main active constituent, has shown direct antioxidant activity via redox reactions and indirect antioxidant activity by inhibiting the activity of free radical producing enzymes 

- and upregulating endogenous antioxidant enzymes, including glutathione. 

- Dandelion is traditionally used in WHM to support healthy liver function and detoxification. It is said Dandelion was used for liver complaints based largely on the doctrine of signatures, because the bright yellow flowers are the colour of a bilious hue[2] . 

- Schisandra is a hepatoprotective herb which supports healthy liver function and liver detoxification processes. It induces phase I enzymes, but is also a powerful inducer of phase II detoxification processes, helping to rapidly clear potentially toxic metabolites generated by phase I. 

- Bupleurum is traditionally used in Chinese medicine to maintain liver health, as a hepatoprotectant and to soothe liver Qi. It is considered to dissolve liver congestion and disperse liver Qi stagnation. 

- Curcumin has been shown to induce phase II liver detoxification enzymes, including glutathione peroxidase, glutathione reductase, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and catalase. 

- Taurine is essential for bile acid function and absorption of lipids. Taurine is preferentially conjugated with bile acids in the liver, which supports the emulsification of dietary fat. 

- Choline and inositol are both components of cell membrane phospholipids and contribute to cell structure and integrity. Choline supports healthy liver function and is essential for lipid and cholesterol transport, while inositol is involved in the transport of fat out of the liver.

- Dandelion is traditionally considered to be both a cholagogue and 

- choleretic, increasing bile production and flow. 

- Dandelion roots are also traditionally considered to be a depurative and alterative, with blood cleansing activity, indicated for chronic skin problems.

Specifically, St Mary’s thistle is traditionally used in WHM to relieve symptoms of dyspepsia, including digestive discomfort, flatulence, bloating and loss of appetite. ## **TECHNICAL INFORMATION** 

- Lung Care contains the herbs Licorice, Elecampane and Adhatoda plus antioxidant nutrients to support lung health and healthy immune system function. 

- Anti-catarrhal herbs reduce the formation of mucus and expectorant herbs facilitate the removal of mucus and other materials from the lungs, bronchi and trachea. Traditionally, there was a strong focus on encouraging elimination to support respiratory system health. It was believed that clearing excess mucus and catarrh would enable optimal respiratory health. 

## Lung health 

- The lungs are two cone-shaped organs that sit in the thoracic cavity and facilitate breathing. In the lungs, small air sacs, called alveoli, are covered in capillaries and allow the exchange of gasses (oxygen and carbon dioxide) between the air and the blood. The average adult lung has approximately 700 million alveoli, with a total surface area of 50-80 square metres (about the size of a tennis court) which allows rapid and efficient gas exchange. Optimal lung function is important as it allows the body to obtain the oxygen needed to meet its cellular demands for nutrients and to remove metabolic waste products. 

- The lungs are continually exposed to inhaled airborne irritants and environmental pollutants, such as cigarette smoke, ozone and pollution, which generate excess reactive oxygen species and are, therefore, vulnerable to the damaging effects of oxidants. To counteract this oxidative threat, the lungs are well-endowed with antioxidant defenses. The respiratory tract lining fluid acts as an interface between the environment, toxic exposure and respiratory tract epithelial cells, and contains high concentrations of antioxidants, including vitamin C, vitamin E and the selenium-dependent enzyme systems, glutathione peroxidase[1] . 

- Inhaled air is full of particles and microorganisms that have potentially damaging effects. Mucus in the airways functions to trap particles from the air, which are then swept upwards towards the pharynx by cilia on the cells lining the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles. 

## Adhatoda 

- Adhatoda is traditionally used in Ayurvedic medicine as an expectorant, to clear respiratory tract mucus, and antispasmodic for respiratory complaints. It is also used in traditional Ayurvedic medicine to relieve coughs and mild fevers. It is known as having kāsaśvāsahara (alleviates breathing difficulties) and 

udarapraśamana (anti-allergenic) actions and is indicated for clearing inflammatory pitta heat and liquefying congestive kapha, for use when there is inflammation from an allergic response to clear the lungs and nostrils. 

- Adhatoda is one of the best-known herbal bronchodilators and respiratory spasmolytics, to help facilitate breathing and relieve chest tightness, breathlessness, non-productive cough and wheezing. 

- The major active constituent in Adhatoda is the alkaloid vasicine. The drug, bromhexine (Bisolvon) was derived from vasicine and is used as an experctorant to aid the thinning and loosening of mucus. 

## Licorice 

- Licorice is traditionally used in Western herbal medicine (WHM) as a demulcent to soothe irritated tissues of the respiratory tract. It acts upon mucous surfaces, lessening irritation, and is useful in dry or catarrhal coughs with inflammation of the lungs and bronchi. 

- Licorice is traditionally used in WHM as an expectorant to clear mucus from the chest and respiratory tract. It is considered a relaxing expectorant as it reduces excess mucus by relaxing spasms to promote natural expectoration. The Commission E approves the use of Licorice root for catarrh of the upper respiratory tract[2] . 

- Licorice is traditionally used in WHM to relieve coughs and bronchial catarrh. Culpeper, a renowned 17[th] century herbalist, said of Licorice: “for those who have a dry cough or hoarseness, wheezing or shortness of breath, and for all the pains of the breast and lungs…”[3] . It is also used in traditional Chinese medicine to relieve coughs.

   - Elecampane is traditionally used in WHM as a lung tonic and to support lung health. It is considered one of the best medicines for pulmonary complaints and its tonifying properties help strengthen the lungs and sustain the strength of the patient with respiratory ailments. ## Immune health 

- Lung Care contains vitamin C, vitamin E and selenium to support healthy immune system function and immune health. 

- Vitamin C concentrations in the body rapidly decline during times of infection and stress. Supplementation with vitamin C can improve components of the immune system including increasing natural killer cell and T-lymphocyte activity, which help to fight infection. 

- Vitamin E is considered one of the most important nutrients for immune cell function. It can increase humoral antibody production, resistance to bacterial infections, cell-mediated immunity, the T-lymphocyte response and natural killer cell activity, thereby playing a role in immunocompetence. 

- Selenium is found in high concentrations in immune tissues, including the liver, spleen and lymph nodes. Cells of the immune system have an important functional need for selenium, as activated T-cells show upregulated selenophosphate synthetase activity, which requires selenium as a building block. 

- Caution in iron overload conditions (e.g. haemochromatosis), as vitamin C increases iron absorption.

- Licorice may cause hypertension, sodium and water retention and hypokalemia through the mineralocorticoid effect of glycyrrhizin (unlikely at this dose). 

- Excessive use of Adhatoda can cause hypotension.

## Antioxidants 

- Antioxidant nutrients, such as vitamins C and E, and selenium, are important for lung health and pulmonary function, as they help protect the lungs from oxidative damage. Vitamins C and E are present in the fluid lining of the lungs where they protect against both endogenous (by-products of metabolism) and external free radicals from the environment, such as ozone and air pollution. 

- Studies have consistently demonstrated a beneficial association between dietary vitamin C and E and ventilatory function[5] . It has been demonstrated that FEV1 (forced expiratory volume) increases by approximately 37mL per 100mg increase in daily vitamin C intake. This increase in FEV is equivalent to the negative effect of approximately 5-10 pack-years of smoking or 1-2 years of aging[6] . 

- Vitamin C is the body’s primary water-soluble antioxidant. It is the major antioxidant in the extracellular fluid lining of the lungs and can help regenerate other antioxidants such as vitamin E. 

- Vitamin C is necessary for collagen and connective tissue synthesis in the respiratory system and may be beneficial for allergic responses due to its natural antihistamine activity. Vitamin C has a dual action against histamine: it prevents the secretion of histamine by white blood cells and increases the detoxification of histamine. 

- Vitamin E is one of the most important and potent lipid-soluble antioxidants in the body due to its oxidative inhibitory action, protecting cell membranes against lipid peroxidation. 

- Selenium has antioxidant activity. It is an essential co-enzyme of glutathione peroxidases and is involved in protecting the body from free radical damage. 

## **DRUG INTERACTIONS** 

- Caution with potassium-depleting drugs (e.g thiazide diuretics and laxatives) and cardiac glycosides - Licorice may increase potassium loss. 

- Caution with corticosteroids - Licorice may potentiate the pharmacologic effects corticosteroid drugs and cause potassium depletion. 

- Caution with warfarin - Licorice can induce CYP450 enzymes and decrease warfarin levels. Monitor INR. 

- Caution with aluminum-based antacids - vitamin C increases the amount of aluminum absorbed. Separate dose by 2 hours. 

## **CAUTIONS** 

- Contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding. 

- Licorice is contraindicated in cholestatic liver disorders, liver cirrhosis, hypertonia, hypokalemia, high blood pressure, cardiovascular disorders and severe kidney insufficiency.

## **TECHNICAL INFORMATION** 

- Lysine is an essential amino acid involved in making proteins in the body and assisting with the metabolism of carbohydrates and fatty acids. Lysine is also an important amino acid required for the biosynthesis of collagen, elastin and carnitine. 

- The human body cannot synthesise lysine, so it must be taken through the diet. The richest sources of lysine are animal proteins, such as meat and poultry, and to a lesser extent, eggs, beans and dairy products. 

## Cold sores 

- Cold sores are painful fluid-filled lesions on or near the lips that are caused by the herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV1). This virus is part of the same family of viruses that causes chickenpox and mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr virus). 

- Cold sore infection is easily transmitted. The virus usually enters a person's body through a break in the skin inside or around the mouth, thus it is often acquired through contact with saliva. Once a person is infected, the virus lays dormant in the nerve cells that supply sensation to the skin. 

- Following a ‘trigger’ event the virus becomes active, and travels through the nerve endings toward the skin’s surface of the lips where it multiplies, causing an outbreak. Whilst the mechanism by which the herpes virus becomes reactivated is currently unknown, cold sore triggers can include exposure to sunlight and wind (especially on the lips), stress and fatigue, infections such as a cold or flu, as well as menstruation and pregnancy. 

## Lysine for cold sore occurrence & symptoms 

- Several double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised controlled trials have demonstrated oral lysine supplementation decreases the frequency of HSV1 outbreaks. 

- Most clinical research on lysine was conducted in the 1980s. However, 

- more recent studies continue to support the original findings. 

- In a small 2008 study, 12 subjects were administered 500mg of lysine daily and monitored monthly over an 8-year period. All participants recorded a reduction in the number of occurrences of lesions as well as the healing time of each lesion[1] . 

- A larger, epidemiological study done in 1983 involving 1543 subjects found that 79% of those surveyed described their symptoms as severe or intolerable without lysine. Without lysine, 90% indicated that healing took place in 6-15 days, but with lysine 83% stated the lesions healed in 5 days or less[2] . 

- Lysine works by having an inhibitory effect on the multiplication of the HSV1. It acts as an antimetabolite by competing with arginine for inclusion in the viral replicative process. Lysine then exerts its effect by retarding the viral growth-promoting action of arginine. 

- Lysine demonstrates greater effectiveness when used in divided doses and taken with a meal containing protein. 

## Collagen health 

- Lysine supports collagen formation and health. 

- Collagen is the protein that forms connective fibres in tissues such as skin, ligaments, cartilage, bones and teeth. As an amino acid, lysine combines with proline and vitamin C to form procollagen. Procollagen is then used to manufacture the four main types of collagen found in different tissues throughout the body. 

## Calcium absorption 

- Lysine supports calcium absorption. 

- In one study, women were given 3g of calcium (as calcium chloride) and either 400mg of lysine or placebo. Both groups demonstrated increased serum calcium levels and increased urinary excretion of calcium, however, the amount of calcium excreted in the lysine group was significantly less than the placebo group, suggesting lysine may suppress calcium excretion in healthy individuals[3] . 

- In a further study of 45 women with osteoporosis the addition of 800mg of lysine to calcium supplementation significantly increased calcium absorption[4] . 

## Immune health 

- Olive leaf is traditionally used in Western herbal medicine to support immune system health and function. 

- The primary constituent of Olive leaf is oleuropein, believed to be responsible for many of the therapeutic properties of the leaf. Olive leaf inhibits the assembly of viruses at the cell membrane, interfering with critical amino acid production, and stops viral shedding. Olive leaf can also inhibit bacteria, either by inactivating cellular enzymes critical for bacterial replication or via attack on the cell membrane[5] .

## **TECHNICAL INFORMATION** 

- Macu-Guard contains Bilberry standardised to anthocyanosides and antioxidant nutrients including lutein and zeaxanthin to support eye health and healthy vision. 

## Eye anatomy 

- The eyes are complex structures made up of the cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina, macula and the optic nerve that allow vision. 

- The lens sits just behind the iris and pupil and helps to focus light on the back of the eye. 

- The retina is the sensory portion of the eye and contains layers of photoreceptors and nerves. Rods are a particular type of photoreceptor, located near the edges of the retina, which are responsible for peripheral and night vision. Cones are photoreceptors that are more central in the retina and are responsible for day and colour vision. Together, rods and cones allow people to see in varying light conditions and different colours. 

- Rod photoreceptors, which contain the visual pigment rhodopsin, lose colour when light strikes them. Pigment regeneration is important to help protect the delicate photoreceptors and maintain vision. 

- The macula (‘yellow spot’) is a small area within the retina that is responsible for central vision and visual acuity. 

## Bilberry 

- Bilberry has a long history of use as a food and medicine for supporting eye health all over the world. 

- The active constituents in Bilberry are anthocyanosides - strong antioxidant compounds that have an affinity for the retinal pigmented epithelium. Bilberry anthocyanosides reinforce the collagen structures of the retina and help protect the eyes from free radical damage. Macu-Guard contains Bilberry, standardised to 25mg anthocyanosides. 

- Bilberry has vasoprotective properties and supports microcirculation to the eye. 

- Bilberry enhances regeneration of rhodopsin in the retina, which is essential for optimal functioning of the rods, light adaptation and night vision[1] . 

## Antioxidant nutrients 

- Vitamin C, the body’s primary water-soluble antioxidant, is found in high concentrations in the eye and maintains clarity of the lens and health of the retina. Vitamin C appears to protect the lens of the eye from free radical damage, directly, due to its antioxidant activity, and indirectly, via its ability to recycle vitamin E. 

- Vitamin E is an important lipid-soluble antioxidant and ample vitamin E may decrease oxidative damage to the lens of the eye. 

- Zinc and copper are essential trace metals that are concentrated in the photoreceptors and the retinal pigment epithelium of the eye. Both zinc and copper are cofactors in a number of ocular enzymes, including copper-zinc superoxide dismutase, which functions as an antioxidant by catalysing the conversion of free radicals to hydrogen peroxide. 

- Long-term, high doses of zinc can reduce the bioavailability of copper. It is recommended that copper intake should also be increased with zinc supplementation. Macu-Guard contains 1mg of copper to maintain copper balance. 

- A 2017 systematic review found that a higher intake of antioxidants (vitamin C, vitamin E, zinc, lutein and anthocyanins) in the diet was associated with longer-term eye health[2] . 

## Lutein & zeaxanthin 

   - Lutein and zeaxanthin are yellow-coloured, xanthophyll carotenoids that are not converted into vitamin A in the body. They are found in high quantities in the retina and macula of the eye and in the lens. Lutein is more prominent at the edges of the retina and in the rods, while zeaxanthin is primarily concentrated in the centre of the retina and the cones. 

   - Lutein and zeaxanthin are powerful antioxidants, helping to protect the eye from oxidative and free radical damage and maintain healthy eyes. 

   - Lutein and zeaxanthin support healthy vision by: 

   - Assisting eye adaptation to variations in light intensity 

   - Helping temporarily relieve light sensitivity and helping the eyes tolerate glaring light 

   - Helping vision recovery after exposure to glaring light 

   - Helping the eyes detect colour contrast 

- Macu-Guard contains key antioxidant nutrients to protect the eyes from oxidative/free radical damage and maintain eye health.

## **Macu-Guard** 

- Lutein and zeaxanthin comprise the macula pigment and are responsible for the characteristic yellow colour of the macula. Lutein and zeaxanthin supplementation increase the level of these carotenoids in the macula, with a corresponding increase in macula pigment optical density (MPOD). A large body of evidence reports a significant relationship between variation in MPOD and visual function[3] . 

- The Lutein Antioxidant Supplementation Trial (LAST) is one of the largest clinical trials to evaluate the impact of lutein on MPOD. Ninety men were given either 10mg of lutein, 10mg lutein with antioxidants or placebo for one year. MPOD increased by 36% in those receiving 10mg lutein and 43% in those receiving lutein plus antioxidants[4] . 

- A double-blind, placebo-controlled study looked at the effects of 10mg of lutein and 2mg of zeaxanthin daily for one year. Results showed MPOD, chromatic contrast and photostress recovery time increased significantly compared to placebo[5] . Another prospective, randomised, open label study found that 10mg of lutein with antioxidants daily significantly increased MPOD and contrast sensitivity (p<0.005) compared to baseline[6] . 

- Macu-Guard contains 10mg of lutein and 2mg of zeaxanthin in a 5:1 ratio. This 5:1 ratio reflects both serum and dietary ratios of these carotenoids. Some evidence suggests that using an equal dose of L:Z can produce poorer results due to duodenal, hepatic or retinal carotenoid competition[7] . 

## **DRUG INTERACTIONS** 

- Caution with aluminium-based antacids – vitamin C increases the amount of aluminium absorbed. Separate doses by at least 2 hours. 

- Caution with anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs - vitamin E may enhance the effects and decrease levels of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (usually only a concern at higher doses). Monitor. 

- Caution with ciclosporin – vitamin E may increase drug absorption. Use under supervision of a health professional. 

- Caution with orlistat – drug may impair absorption of vitamin E. Separate dose by 2 hours. 

- Caution with NSAIDs, cephalexin and tetracyclines and quinolone antibiotics – zinc forms complexes with these drugs and may reduce drug effectiveness. Separate dose by 3 hours. 

## **CAUTIONS** 

- Contraindicated in Wilson’s disease – a rare inherited disorder of copper storage in which biliary excretion of copper is impaired. 

- Caution with iron overload conditions, such as hemochromatosis, as vitamin C increases iron absorption. 

## **SIDE EFFECTS** 

- None noted at the recommended dose. 

## Blue light 

- Blue light is a colour in the visible light spectrum that can be seen by the human eye. Blue light waves are among the shortest and highest energy wavelengths and, therefore, the most damaging. Prolonged exposure to blue light has been linked to eyestrain, headaches, mental fatigue and retinal damage. 

- Sources of blue light include digital screens (TVs, computers, smart phones and tablets) and fluorescent and LED lighting. Many people spend the majority of their waking hours staring at a screen, whether it be a computer, phone or TV, which puts them at an increased risk of the damaging effects of blue light. 

## **COMPANION PRODUCTS** 

   - Ginkgo Biloba 6000 

   - Grape Seed Gold 

   - Resveratrol AdvantAGE 

   - Triple Strength Omega-3 

- Lutein and zeaxanthin filter harmful, high-energy blue light. They serve as ‘natural sunglasses’ that act as an optical filter for blue light, reducing chromatic aberration and preventing damage to the photoreceptor cell layer . Their ability to absorb or filter blue light can be measured as MPOD. MPOD is directly related to the quantity of lutein and zeaxanthin in the macula. 

## AREDS 

- Macu-Guard contains antioxidant nutrients, vitamin C, vitamin E, zinc, copper, lutein and zeaxanthin, that have been studied for reducing the risk of declining macular health. 

- The Age-Related Eye Disease Studies 1 & 2 (AREDS1[8] and AREDS2[9] ) are the largest studies to-date on eye health, sponsored by the National Eye Institute. These studies found supplementing with high levels of antioxidants (vitamin C, vitamin E, lutein, zeaxanthin and zinc) significantly reduced the risk of declining macular health. 

- AREDS2 found that 25mg of zinc was as effective as the original 80mg that was studied in AREDS1. Data suggests that this dose may be the maximal level of zinc that can be absorbed and is less likely to contribute to some of the side-effects seen with high-dose supplementation, including alterations in copper homoeostasis. 

- Macu-Guard contains 10mg of lutein, 2mg of zeaxanthin and 25mg of zinc to match the doses studied in AREDS2 as well as vitamin C, vitamin E and copper.

## **TECHNICAL INFORMATION** 

- Magnesium Chewable is an innovative supplement combining two organic, bioavailable forms of magnesium in a chewable tablet. Many people have difficulty swallowing large tablets or capsules, which can limit compliance with supplements, especially minerals like magnesium that are required in higher doses. Magnesium Chewable is a delicious raspberry flavoured tablet that can be chewed to increase compliance and enable supplementation with high-dose magnesium. 

- Magnesium Chewable contains two organic forms of magnesium that are well absorbed in the body. 

- A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in 46 healthy volunteers compared the relative absorbability and bioequivalence of three forms of magnesium - oxide, citrate and amino acid chelate - under acute and chronic conditions. Results showed that organic forms (magnesium citrate and amino acid chelate) were better absorbed than inorganic magnesium oxide[1] . 

## Magnesium 

- Magnesium is an essential nutrient for over 600 enzymatic processes in the body, required for energy production, muscle contraction and relaxation, cardiac rhythm, vascular tone, carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism, bone formation, neurological function and brain function. 

- Optimal magnesium intake is considered to be 320mg a day for women and 420mg a day for men[2] , however, many individuals are not consuming adequate amounts. According to the Australian Health Survey, one in three people aged two years and over (37% of males and 34% of females) did not meet their estimated dietary requirements for magnesium[3] . 

- Magnesium is found in green leafy vegetables, nuts, seeds, whole grains and cacao. Today’s farming and agricultural practices have led to a decline in the magnesium content in foods, with estimates that magnesium content has decreased by as much as 80-90% in vegetables such as lettuce and spinach[4] . Modern dietary practices, such as cooking and bleaching grain, causes a loss of up to 80% of magnesium content. Additionally, diets high in calcium, sodium and phosphorus (found in soft drink) or low in selenium, vitamin B6 and vitamin D can reduce magnesium absorption. Foods high in phytates, polyphenols and oxalic acid, such as rice and nuts, can bind to magnesium to produce insoluble complexes, reducing magnesium availability and 

absorption. Moreover, consumption of caffeine and alcohol can lower magnesium levels by increasing renal excretion. 

- Under normal dietary conditions, about 30% of ingested magnesium is absorbed. Magnesium homeostasis is maintained via the intestine (facilitating magnesium absorption), the bone (magnesium storage) and the kidneys (excretion). The largest amount of magnesium is stored in bone (50-60%), muscle (20-30%) and other soft tissues (20%). 

- Due to magnesium’s role in energy production, cardiorespiratory function and muscle function, physically active individuals have higher magnesium requirements[5] . Strenuous exercise can also result in increased urinary and sweat losses of magnesium, increasing magnesium requirements by approximately 10-20%[6] . 

- Magnesium deficiency can produce non-specific symptoms, with the most common symptoms being muscle cramps, spasms or twitching. Other symptoms include fatigue, headaches, sleep disturbances, anxiety and irritability. 

- Magnesium Chewable helps prevent dietary magnesium deficiency. 

## Muscle health 

- Magnesium is an essential nutrient for muscle health and muscle contraction function. Magnesium works with calcium for muscle contraction and relaxation. Magnesium is a calcium antagonist, competing with calcium for binding sites. In the resting state, magnesium is present in concentrations 10 000 times higher than calcium in muscle cells. When the message comes for a muscle to contract, calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and binds to troponin C and myosin to induce contraction. When magnesium levels are insufficient, not as much calcium is required to displace magnesium, resulting in muscle cramps and spasms. 

- Magnesium Chewable can help relieve muscle cramps and reduce the occurrence of muscle cramps when dietary intake is inadequate. 

## Energy production & glucose metabolism 

   - Magnesium supports energy production as it is involved in the metabolism of carbohydrates and fats to produce energy and is critical for the manufacture of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) within cells. ATP exists primarily as a complex with magnesium (MgATP).

- Magnesium is an important cofactor in glucose metabolism and glycaemic control. It is essential for insulin receptor phosphorylation and regulates glucose uptake in muscle[7] . 

## Nervous system health 

- Magnesium supports healthy nervous system function as it is required for nerve conduction. It modulates the hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis and can reduce the release of adrenalin and noradrenalin, supporting a healthy stress response in the body. 

- Stress may increase magnesium loss, and in a vicious cycle, magnesium deficiency increases the body’s susceptibility to stress. Clinical studies show low magnesium status in stressed and anxious individuals, with magnesium deficiency found in up to 45%-60% of stressed subjects[8] . 

## Cardiovascular health 

- Magnesium helps maintain cardiovascular system health and heart health. It is essential for cardiac muscle contraction and the production of energy within the heart muscle. Magnesium plays a role in the active transport of calcium and potassium ions across cell membranes, which is essential for nerve impulse conduction, muscle contraction and normal heart rhythm. It is also essential for the contractility of vascular smooth muscle cells in the arterial wall and influences endothelial function, thereby influencing vasodilation and vasoconstriction. 

## Bone health 

- Magnesium supports bone health and assists in the development and maintenance of bones and teeth. Approximately 50-60% of total body magnesium stores reside in the bone, where it binds at the surface of the hydroxyapatite crystals. Magnesium in bones serves as a reservoir of magnesium, which can be released from bone to maintain physiological extracellular concentrations when magnesium intake is low. 

## Menstrual cramps & spasms 

- Magnesium Chewable can help relieve symptoms of premenstrual tension (PMT) including menstrual cramps and spasms and dysmenorrhoea. 

## **DRUG INTERACTIONS** 

- Caution with quinolone antibiotics – magnesium forms insoluble complexes with quinolones, decreasing drug absorption. Take drug 2 hours before or 6 hours after magnesium. 

- Caution with tetracycline antibiotics – tetracyclines form insoluble complexes with magnesium, reducing absorption of both. Separate dose by at least 3 hours. 

- Caution with bisphosphonates – magnesium can form complexes with drug and reduce absorption. Separate dose by 2 hours. 

- Caution with calcium channel blockers and other hypotensive medication – magnesium may have additive effects and enhance the hypotensive effect. Monitor blood pressure. 

- Caution with potassium-sparing diuretics – these drugs also have magnesium-sparing properties which could, theoretically, lead to increased magnesium levels. Monitor. 

- Caution with skeletal muscle relaxants – magnesium can potentiate effects. 

## **CAUTIONS** 

- High dose magnesium is contraindicated in people with compromised renal function and heart block. 

- Caution in individuals with low blood pressure – magnesium supplementation can lower blood pressure. Monitor. 

## **SIDE EFFECTS** 

- Magnesium can cause gastrointestinal irritation, nausea and diarrhoea in sensitive individuals, however, usually in much higher doses.

- Dysmenorrhoea is defined as painful uterine cramps that precede or accompany menses and is caused by hypercontractility of the myometrium and arteriolar vasoconstriction. Magnesium can help alleviate this via its muscle relaxation and vasodilation activity as well as by inhibiting the biosynthesis of prostaglandin F2 (PGF2) alpha. 

- A systematic review of three small studies found that overall magnesium supplementation was more effective than placebo for pain relief and reduced the need for additional medication[9] . 

- There are no clear dosage recommendations, as studies use different dosage regimes, however, magnesium appears to be effective when taken daily, or taken between one and seven days prior to menses and for the first two or three days of menstruation. 

- Current research suggests that at least two months’ supplementation are required to see a benefit in other symptoms of PMT[10] . A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled cross over study investigated the effects of 200mg of magnesium as magnesium oxide for 2 menstrual cycles. In the second month, there was a greater reduction (p=0.009) in symptoms including weight gain, swelling of extremities, breast tenderness and abdominal bloating[11] .

- Magnesium supports a healthy pregnancy as it is an essential nutrient for a range of biological reactions in the body and has a structural role in bone formation. 

- Pregnancy increases magnesium requirements. The recommend daily intake of magnesium increases from 320mg to between 350 and 400mg per day during pregnancy[12] .

## Mild migraines 

- Magnesium Citrate 900 can help reduce the occurrence of mild migraines. Higher doses of magnesium are needed over a longer period of time, with studies finding 600mg of elemental magnesium can help reduce migraine attack frequency after 3 months of supplementation. 

- A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in migraine sufferers found that supplementation with 600mg of magnesium (as citrate) decreased migraine attack frequency (p=0.005) and severity (p<0.001) compared to placebo[5] .
